newsitem.title: UK: Small promises give Britain's Labour big poll lead.
newsitem.headline: Small promises give Britain's Labour big poll lead.

text.p: Most politicians run for office promising the earth. Tony Blair is courting British voters by telling them not to expect too much.

Blair, whose opposition Labour party is hot favourite to win the May 1 election, has based his appeal on a belief that voters are disillusioned with the ruling Conservatives because Prime Minister John Major was unable to keep all the promises he made at the 1992 election, especially on taxes.
"The Conservatives' broken promises taint all politics. That is why we have made it our guiding rule not to promise what we cannot deliver," Labour's manifesto says.
Blair's minimalism, which polls suggest is striking a chord with voters, was on show at a public meeting on Friday in Kidsgrove, a textile and farming seat in central England.
In the course of an hour's questioning, he refused perhaps a dozen times to make commitments that would have cost money.

Appeals for free eye and dental checks, for drugs to treat multiple sclerosis, for a new road, for new student grants, for small businesses and for more generous pensions were all turned down, politely but firmly.
Public finances were in such a mess after 18 years of Conservative profligacy that Britain simply could not afford such largesse, Blair argued.
"I can't promise you..."
"Again, I can't make a specific commitment..."
"I tell you: I'm not going to spin you what's a lie, which is that we can put everything right overnight and it can all be done by taxpayers' money. It cannot," he said.
Joe Klein, the author of "Primary Colours", a thinly fictionalised account of President Bill Clinton's 1992 campaign for the White House, is among those struck by Blair's approach.
"Clinton is more eager to please," Klein, who has joined Blair's travelling press party for the New Yorker, commented.
The abandonment of the tax-and-spend policies that have cost Labour four successive elections since 1979 has dismayed many left-wing traditionalists.
But conversations with some of the 400 people who managed to get tickets for the meeting at Kidsgrove town hall suggested that Blair is catching the public mood.

"I just think the Tories have become stagnant. I just don't think there's anything they can offer any more," said David Moorhouse, 28, who voted for the Conservatives at the 1992 election but said he would probably vote Labour on May 1.
"I'm swinging more red than blue," he said.
Moorhouse says he is sick of "sleaze", the catch-all word for the sex scandals and financial improprieties that have tainted a score of Conservative ministers and parliamentarians.

Sleaze is also one of the issues -- along with the government's record on health and law and order -- swaying Mary Hebblethwaite, 69. "These politicians are in the public eye and they should behave accordingly," she said.
Her friend Joan Gater, a life-long Conservative voter also 69, said she also planned to desert the ruling party in the hope that Blair can provide her with a better pension.
"He can't do any worse," she said. "The Tories have been in too long and we've got to give Labour a chance to show what they can do."

Lynne Robertson, 77, is unhappy about sleaze but the main reason she plans to switch to Labour is the government's handling of the crisis over mad cow disease, which she said was threatening her family farm with bankruptcy.
"I've voted Tory all my life, and my family has before me, but for what they've done to the farmers, they deserve to go," she said.
"Switchers" such as these explain why Labour leads the Conservatives in opinion polls by about 20 percentage points.
And after listening to Blair, they cannot say they have not been warned: Labour will not meet their pent-up demands overnight.
Blair, in the jargon of British politics, has got his betrayal in first.
